Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later

Junwei Yao yao.junw@northeastern.edu Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Yongxi Zhou zhou.yongx@northeastern.edu Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Zike Yang zikeyang@alumni.usc.edu Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Zhijun Wang g674901087@gmail.com Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Jianan Liu jiananliu2408@gmail.com Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Yanxian Chen chen.yanx@northeastern.edu Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Wenbo Ye ywb6113@gmail.com Affiliation: Independent Researcher
Abstract

Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion’s share of the evidence’s content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on τ\tau-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.

††footnotetext: AI assistance: The authors used Claude Code (Anthropic) during the preparation of this work.

1 Introduction

Applications that call a language model many times, such as agents, assistants and multi-step pipelines, carry text from one call to the next: documents read so far, conversation turns, tool outputs. We call this text the state. Every call pays for it in tokens and the context window bounds it, so applications compact it: they delete parts of it to fit a budget. At compaction time the application usually knows its current question, and the natural choice is to keep what that question needs. The state, however, outlives that question. Later questions, unknown when the deletion was made, must be answered from whatever survived, and a deleted sentence is gone for all of them. We call the question available at compaction time known and the later ones hidden. Query-aware compressors are usually evaluated on the question they compress for; we evaluate them on the hidden ones.

We compare query-aware selection, which keeps what the known question needs, with question-agnostic compressors. Our main instance uses typed decision models, which take a state and typed questions about it (a Boolean, a Choice among options or a Score) and return a probability for each answer (TypeSafe AI, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). Typed selection asks one Boolean per sentence, “is this sentence needed to answer the question?”, and keeps the most probable sentences; the same model then answers the questions, and in this role we call it the reader. Figure 1 shows the risk. We compare it with random deletion, question-agnostic selection by the same model, TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) selection and lead (the first sentences). We also run LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024), which deletes individual words without any question, and, at token budgets, LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) and maximal marginal relevance (MMR; Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998), two established compressors that use the question. The corpora are MultiRC (Khashabi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019), ERASER’s FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018; DeYoung et al., 2020), Evidence Inference (Lehman et al., 2019) and LoCoMo conversation memory (Maharana et al., 2024), in which several questions share one text and each question’s evidence is annotated, and recorded τ\tau-bench agent trajectories (Yao et al., 2024), whose questions ask for the identifiers that later tool calls pass. Our findings are:

  • •

    Selection for the known question beats random deletion on that question. On MultiRC, typed selection, MMR and LongLLMLingua raise known-question accuracy over random deletion at 25%, but none shows a detected advantage on hidden questions on average. On MultiRC, hidden questions gain only where they share the known question’s evidence. On FEVER, a gain in recovering a claim’s label is not detected when the kept text is scored for what it supports (Section 3). The label-accuracy gain of word-level compression there is not shown to rest on the kept text either (Section 4).

  • •

    On MultiRC, picking words beats picking sentences by the same scores. With the same importance scores, picking words instead of sentences raises hidden-question accuracy, and LLMLingua-2 and a hybrid of typed sentences and LLMLingua-2 words lead on hidden questions. They keep about as many evidence words as random deletion but far more of the evidence’s content words, which partly explains the lead: at equal content-word retention it shrinks from 12.5 to 7.3 points with gpt-6-luna (Section 4).

  • •

    The ordering is not stable across settings. On Evidence Inference typed selection beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, typed selection beats random deletion and LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain (Section 5).

Concurrent work shows that compaction can serve the current query and fail later ones (Liu et al., 2026; Zhang, 2026). We add an evaluation on annotated evidence that compares sentence- and word-level compression and locates where each serves later questions.

2 Evaluation setup

This section describes the MultiRC experiment; Sections 3 and 5 give the changes for the other settings.

Data and models.

Each MultiRC question has several candidate answers that annotators labeled correct or incorrect, and a question can have more than one correct answer. We use 300 paragraphs with at least three questions and 6–20 sentences, with 3,355 questions and 17,895 candidate answers, from the validation and training splits (validation alone has too few such paragraphs). The first listed question of each paragraph is known and the others are hidden. gpt-6-luna reads every corpus. Every gpt-6-luna read and selection in this paper goes through the OpenAI Decisions API (OpenAI, 2026), the typed decision interface: a request poses typed questions and returns a probability for each answer, with no generated text. Three open-weight models built for the typed decision interface, open-decider (2B), open-bosun (1.7B) and open-lumma (0.6B) (Mapika, 2026; Hanno Labs, 2026; FrontiersMind, 2026), also read MultiRC from their released weights, and qwen3.8-flash is a general instruction-tuned reader (Appendix B). We drop refused answers; counting them as wrong instead changes neither the sign of any typed −- random contrast nor whether its interval excludes zero (Appendix B).

Selectors and budgets.

Both model-based selectors ask one Boolean per sentence, with the sentences numbered in the state. Typed selection puts the known question in the state and asks “is sentence ii needed to answer the question?”. Question-agnostic selection gives no question and asks “does sentence ii state a fact that a reader is likely to be asked about later?”. A policy keeps a budget b∈{25,50,75}%b\in\{25,50,75\}\% of a paragraph’s sentences (rounded half to even, at least one). Typed and agnostic selection keep the most probable sentences, TF-IDF selection those closest to the known question, lead the first ones, and random deletion one seeded uniform sample. Kept sentences stay in document order. Token-matched tests cut every text, LLMLingua-2’s included, to the same o200k token count (Appendix G).

Reading and measures.

One request asks one Boolean per candidate answer: “given the passage, is this a correct answer to the question?”, where “no” is defined as “not supported or incorrect”. Once a compaction deletes the evidence for a correct answer, the reader is therefore asked to reject that answer. We score each candidate answer against the MultiRC labels, average within each paragraph, then over paragraphs, with paragraph-bootstrap 95% intervals; a difference is detected when its interval excludes zero. Answering “no” to every candidate already scores 55.6%, and of the four typed readers only gpt-6-luna (88.2%) and open-decider (75.3%) are detectably above it on the full text, so the main tables report these two. A hidden question is overlapping if its annotated evidence shares a sentence with the known question’s, and disjoint otherwise.

Prespecified analyses.

Hypotheses, tests and decision rules were specified before any model request for the Evidence Inference overlap test, the KEEP–DROP contrast, the LoCoMo test and four follow-ups under one plan (token-matched budgets, query-aware baselines, three-way labels and harder LoCoMo options). The same holds for the LLMLingua-2 granularity test, the hybrid compactor, a test with a different known question, a general-reader test, the τ\tau-bench test and the abstractive-summary test. Appendix A counts the outcomes and lists every prediction that was not fully met. The other analyses, including the content-word analysis and the FEVER evidence-support check of Section 4, are exploratory. The ancillary files contain the summary tables and the values of all reported numbers.

3 Selection for the known question beats random deletion on that question

The known question gains.

At a 25% budget, open-decider answers the known question at 70% after typed selection, against 61% after random deletion and 74% on the full text; for gpt-6-luna the same accuracies are 77%, 67% and 89% (compacted texts in Table 1).

Averaged over hidden questions, selection stays near random deletion.

Typed −- random hidden accuracy is slightly below zero for both readers at 25% and 50%, and question-agnostic selection is similarly close to random (Table 1). The split holds when texts are cut to the same token count: typed −- random at 25% with gpt-6-luna is +11.4 [+9.1, +13.8] points on the known question and −-0.4 [−-1.5, +0.6] on hidden ones. LongLLMLingua and MMR show the same split with both readers, and on hidden questions LongLLMLingua falls below random deletion (−-1.6 [−-2.6, −-0.6] with gpt-6-luna; Appendix G). With qwen3.8-flash as reader, typed −- random is +10.4 [+7.4, +13.3] on the known question and −-0.6 [−-1.8, +0.6] on hidden ones.

Hidden questions gain where they share the known question’s evidence.

ERASER (DeYoung et al., 2020) marks evidence sentences for 3,300 of the 3,355 MultiRC questions. Typed selection at 25% keeps 50% of the known question’s evidence (gpt-6-luna) against 25% expected for a random subset, and about the random share for hidden questions. Hidden questions that share evidence with the known one gain +4.3 [+2.2, +6.4] points (gpt-6-luna) and +5.3 [+2.9, +7.7] (open-decider). Disjoint ones lose −-2.9 [−-4.3, −-1.4] and −-3.0 [−-4.5, −-1.4], with less of their evidence kept than under random deletion (18% against 25%; Figure 2).

Deleted evidence drives the losses.

A hidden answer that was right on the full text flips more often when its evidence was deleted. With gpt-6-luna, adding some of the deleted evidence back undoes more flips than adding as many sentences that are evidence for no question (+26.8 [+22.6, +31.5] points; Appendix D). A sufficiency check (“does the passage contain the information needed to answer this question?”) ranks questions with broken evidence first. Yet re-reading a random quarter of hidden questions on the full text recovers most of what re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter does (Appendix D).

FEVER and Evidence Inference: hidden claims gain in label recovery.

Each question here is a claim, and the reader judges whether the text supports it. We sample 200 FEVER documents with 5,433 hidden claims and 792 Evidence Inference clinical-trial articles (Appendix E); the first claim of each document is known. On FEVER at 25% typed −- random hidden-claim accuracy is +17.2 points, and on Evidence Inference disjoint claims gain too, with more of their evidence kept than random deletion keeps (Figure 2).

Label recovery and support scoring disagree.

Label accuracy counts the document’s label as right even when a claim’s evidence was deleted. A prespecified three-way read therefore also scores each answer against what the kept text supports: the document’s label if all of the claim’s annotated evidence was kept and “not enough info” if all of it was deleted. In this read, with true and false claims weighted equally, typed selection on FEVER recovers the label 25.2 points more often than random deletion, while its support-target accuracy, with the three targets weighted equally, differs from random deletion by −-1.0 [−-3.9, +2.2] points (Appendix J). Prespecified KEEP–DROP tests give a hidden claim two texts with the same number of sentences, one with its evidence and one without; KEEP beats DROP by +50.0 [+47.4, +52.4] points on FEVER and +17.8 [+15.9, +19.7] on Evidence Inference (Appendix K).

For sentence selection, the gain follows the extra evidence kept.

Across the eight 25% groups of Figure 2 (corpus, reader, overlapping or disjoint), the typed −- random hidden gain rises with how much more of the hidden questions’ evidence typed selection keeps than random deletion, at 0.370.37 points of gain per point of extra evidence. We fixed this line before a second experiment that repeats typed selection with a different, randomly drawn known question in every document. On the eight new groups it misses the observed gains by 3.4 points on average. The largest misses are 9.5 points (overlapping FEVER claims, under-predicted) and 6.9 (overlapping MultiRC questions read by open-decider, over-predicted); the other six are within 4.8 points (Appendix F).

4 On MultiRC, word-level compression serves later questions

LLMLingua-2 scores every word of the text without any question and keeps the highest-scoring words. A prespecified hybrid keeps typed whole sentences up to half the token budget and fills the rest with the highest-scoring LLMLingua-2 words of the other sentences (Appendix H). Table 2 compares them with sentence selection at 25% of the tokens.

Word-level compression leads on hidden questions.

LLMLingua-2 −- random sentence deletion on hidden questions with annotated evidence, from the model of Appendix I without retention terms, is +12.5 [+11.3, +13.6] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna, +6.0 [+4.7, +7.3] with open-decider and +21.0 [+18.7, +23.4] in label accuracy on FEVER; the paired contrast over all hidden questions, dropping refusals pairwise, gives +12.1 and +21.0 for the two gpt-6-luna cells (Appendix G). LLMLingua-2 is also ahead of typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells (Table 2). The hybrid beats typed selection on hidden questions in all three cells, by 4.6 to 8.3 points with every interval above zero; it beats LLMLingua-2 on FEVER and stays below it on MultiRC (Appendix H).

The gain comes from picking words.

A prespecified test keeps the LLMLingua-2 scores and changes only the unit kept. Picking words instead of whole sentences raises hidden-question accuracy at 25% by +11.7 points (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna), +4.6 (MultiRC, open-decider) and +19.1 (FEVER). Whole sentences picked by the same scores are not detectably better than random sentence deletion in five of six cells (Appendix H). On the known MultiRC question LLMLingua-2 is ahead of typed selection with gpt-6-luna in all four comparisons. The two intervals at sentence budgets exclude zero, and the one at 50% of the tokens just does (upper end −0.02-0.02 points) (Appendices G and H).

Word-level compression keeps the evidence’s content words.

Counted over all words, LLMLingua-2, the hybrid and random sentence deletion keep similar shares of the hidden questions’ evidence on MultiRC, yet their accuracies differ by up to 12.5 points. Sentence deletion keeps a sentence’s content and function words together. LLMLingua-2 drops function words first, so it keeps 48.0% of the evidence’s content words against 26.1% for random sentence deletion (Table 2). For sentence policies the two counts agree within half a point, so the relation of Section 3 is unchanged.

Content-word retention accounts for part of the lead.

A model of each answer’s correctness, with document fixed effects, compares policies at equal content-word retention. It describes an association, since the policies produce the retention they are compared at. At equal retention the MultiRC LLMLingua-2 −- random-sentence gap shrinks from 12.5 to +7.3 [+6.1, +8.4] points with gpt-6-luna and from 6.0 to +2.0 [+0.7, +3.2] with open-decider. Also conditioning on how many of each candidate answer’s content words survive leaves +4.9 points with gpt-6-luna and +0.6 [−-0.5, +1.8] with open-decider. The hybrid −- typed gaps shrink the same way (Table 15). On FEVER binned retention leaves 1.3 points; a linear term leaves 14.9, because accuracy rises non-linearly with retention there.

Which words are kept matters too.

On FEVER typed selection keeps more of the hidden claims’ content words than LLMLingua-2 yet scores lower (Table 2). At the same content-word retention LLMLingua-2 still beats random word deletion by +6.7 [+5.5, +8.0] points on MultiRC with gpt-6-luna, +1.7 [+0.5, +2.9] with open-decider and +9.6 [+7.5, +11.7] on FEVER (Appendix I).

LLM-written summaries stay below word-level compression.

A compaction can also have an LLM rewrite the text. Two summarizers, qwen3.8-flash and gpt-6.1-sol, summarized each MultiRC paragraph within the same token budget, once for unknown later questions and once for the known question (Appendix O). On hidden questions the generic summaries beat random sentence deletion by 7.6 and 10.9 points but stay below LLMLingua-2: summary −- LLMLingua-2 is −-4.5 [−-5.7, −-3.2] and −-1.3 [−-2.4, −-0.3] points. The summaries written for the known question answer it better than typed selection and LLMLingua-2 (88.5% and 89.2%), but on hidden questions they fall below random deletion (qwen3.8-flash, −-2.9 [−-4.0, −-1.8]) or show no detected gain (gpt-6.1-sol, +0.9 [−-0.2, +2.1]).

On FEVER, label accuracy overstates the word-level gain.

FEVER accuracy counts the document’s label, which Section 3 shows can be right without textual support. The LLMLingua-2 gain over random sentence deletion lies on true claims (+31.5 [+28.0, +35.0] points; false claims −-2.2 [−-3.7, −-1.0]). When at most a fifth of a true claim’s evidence content words survive, the reader still calls it supported for 56.0% of claims after LLMLingua-2 and 26.8% after random sentence deletion. An evidence-support target, scored on the binary reads, reproduces the three-way result for typed −- random (−-0.2 [−-3.4, +3.0] points, label-balanced) and removes the hybrid’s gain over typed selection (−-3.7 [−-9.4, +1.3]). Under LLMLingua-2 it is undefined for 99% of hidden claims, whose evidence is partly kept, so its FEVER gain is not shown to rest on the kept text (Appendix I).

5 The ordering is not stable: Evidence Inference and agent states

Evidence Inference.

On Evidence Inference typed selection keeps more of even the disjoint claims’ evidence than random deletion (Figure 2). It beats LLMLingua-2 on hidden claims when LLMLingua-2 is set to the compression rate of 25% sentence deletion (+12.2 [+10.1, +14.4] points); at the 50% rate the difference is +1.0 [−-0.5, +2.6]. This comparison is not token-matched: at 25% the typed texts keep 28.9% of the article’s o200k tokens and the LLMLingua-2 texts 25.8% (Appendices G and L).

Agent trajectories.

In the recorded τ\tau-bench retail trajectories an agent calls tools for a simulated user. The state is a trajectory up to its middle tool output, split into turns, tool calls and tool outputs. The known question asks which identifier (an order, item, product or payment-method ID, or a zip code) the next tool call passes; each hidden question asks the same for a later call, among same-shaped identifiers from the state. On 390 states with 837 hidden questions at 25% of the tokens, typed −- random is +22.3 [+15.1, +28.9] points with gpt-6-luna and +21.7 [+15.7, +27.6] with qwen3.8-flash, while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain (+4.0 [−-1.1, +9.3]); token-level extractive compressors are known to strip the action syntax that agents need (Zhang & Sun, 2026). Typed selection keeps the hidden question’s identifier for 66.4% of hidden questions against 42.4% (random) and 52.3% (LLMLingua-2).

Anticipating later calls costs the known one.

Selectors that anticipate later calls trade the known call for the hidden ones: on a 120-state subsample, expected-coverage selection gains +12.8 [+5.2, +20.8] points over typed selection on hidden questions and −-10.6 (90% interval [−-17.8, −-2.9]) on the known one. About half of the hidden gain comes from fewer refusals: scored on answered questions only, it is +5.8 [−-1.4, +13.6] (Appendix N).

Conversation memory.

LoCoMo’s ten long conversations are compacted four times as they grow, so a dropped turn never returns. At the last checkpoint, a typed 25% memory with a hidden question’s evidence beats one with the same number of turns without it by 13.3 points (gpt-6-luna), in all 10 conversations. Typed versus random deletion is unresolved for both readers, and on the four-choice format empty memory already scores 81.4% (Appendix M).

6 Discussion

Query-aware sentence selection raises the known question’s accuracy over random deletion. On later questions it helps those that share the known question’s evidence. On MultiRC, where many do not, it does no better than random deletion on average.

On MultiRC the compressors that lead on later questions delete words. They drop function words first, so the same token budget holds more of the evidence’s content words. At equal content-word retention two fifths to two thirds of LLMLingua-2’s MultiRC lead over random sentence deletion disappears, and LLMLingua-2 still beats random words, so which words are kept also matters. On FEVER, typed selection’s label gain is not detected under support scoring, and the word-level gain is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ordering is not general. On Evidence Inference, where even disjoint claims keep more evidence under typed selection, it beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget. On agent trajectories, whose later calls need exact identifiers, LLMLingua-2 keeps fewer of them than typed selection and shows no detected gain.

For evaluation, the results suggest scoring hidden questions as well as the known one, comparing with random deletion at matched tokens, measuring the hidden questions’ evidence kept in content words, and reporting support-based scoring next to label recovery. Compaction also costs tokens to build: for typed selection at 25% with gpt-6-luna, compacting once pays for itself in input tokens only with one request per later question, after about 6.6 to 11.0 of them on FEVER, Evidence Inference and LoCoMo. On Evidence Inference this is more than its mean of 3.7 later questions, and on MultiRC the extrapolated break-even, 14.0, exceeds its mean of 10.2 (Appendix L). Keeping the full state allows a re-read for a later question, but neither recovery we tested matches it. On MultiRC, re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter of hidden questions on the full text lifts accuracy over all hidden questions from 67% to 74%, against 89% on the full text (Appendix D). On agent trajectories, fetching dropped units on demand reaches 69.1% against 88.8% for the full state at 102.0% of its passage tokens, and the prespecified prediction that it would come close is not met (Appendix N).

7 Related work

Prompt compression removes tokens or sentences by perplexity (Jiang et al., 2023), by query-aware importance (Jiang et al., 2024) or by a learned task-agnostic importance (Pan et al., 2024), and key–value (KV) cache compression has the same split (Kim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Earlier agent-memory work studied the same write-before-query asymmetry. TierMem (Zhu et al., 2026) falls back to a raw log when a router judges pre-query summaries insufficient, and EMBER (Li et al., 2026) learns which evidence to retain before the query. Chen et al. (2026) find that query-aware KV eviction does not generalize across queries, and Yu et al. (2026) separate write-time from retrieval-time loss. We delete sentences (turns on LoCoMo) for one known question and test the questions hidden at deletion time with annotated evidence and KEEP–DROP substitutions. The closest work is concurrent. Tirmazi et al. (2026) formalize compaction against later queries, with a set-membership case study, and Liu et al. (2026) find that compacting agent KV caches before later queries arrive hurts, and that deferring compaction recovers much of the cost; RestoreKV (Baek et al., 2026) adds learned restoration to query-agnostic eviction, and Luo et al. (2026) find that hiding the question at compression time reorders KV-cache compressors, with most no better than trivial baselines. These work on KV caches rather than on evidence-annotated text. Liu (2026) counts the extra retrieval calls an agent makes to re-acquire state that compression dropped, and Zhang (2026) tests whether compressed memory keeps what a later update needs on synthetic histories; we measure answer accuracy on later questions of existing corpora and locate the loss with evidence annotations. Wang et al. (2026) find that context compactors keep about a sixth of the constraints a user sets for the agent’s later behavior. Sadowski & Chudziak (2026) and Shen & Li (2026) optimize what is written when the later goal is known. Mnemon (Wang, 2026) uses the same per-record “is this needed” Boolean but keeps its raw records recoverable. Shankaranarayana et al. (2026) find that asking whether the evidence suffices is more informative than answer confidence; we ask it after compaction has deleted part of the evidence. Ai et al. (2026) find that KV-cache eviction can keep final-answer accuracy while the reasoning that supports the answer degrades; on FEVER we find the analogous gap between label accuracy and the evidence the kept text retains.

8 Limitations

The experiments use public text and conversation benchmarks and recorded agent trajectories, not live agents. Abstractive summaries are tested only on MultiRC at a 25% budget. In the τ\tau-bench test the actions and tool outputs are fixed by the recording, the questions ask only for identifiers, retail is the only domain with enough trajectories for inference, and the only budget is 25%. The relation between gain and evidence kept is tested by consistency across settings, KEEP–DROP interventions and one out-of-sample check on the three document corpora, for sentence selection; it could not be assessed on LoCoMo and holds only qualitatively on τ\tau-bench. The content-word analysis of word-level compression is exploratory, leaves part of the MultiRC gap unexplained and, on FEVER, does not separate content words from all words. The model-based sentence selectors are typed models, which usually also answer; qwen3.8-flash is the only general instruction-tuned reader, and it reads the texts that gpt-6-luna selected. Only two typed readers perform above the all-“no” baseline on MultiRC. On the three document corpora the known question is the first listed one or, in one test, one other randomly drawn question per document. Evidence annotations are incomplete, so neither the retention tests nor the evidence-support target can account for unannotated evidence.

Budgets count sentences or conversation turns, except in the token-matched tests and the τ\tau-bench test; Appendix L counts input tokens. The KEEP–DROP comparison covers one budget and does not include MultiRC. LoCoMo has ten conversations and a four-choice format on which empty memory already scores 81.4%. Hosted reads taken at different times can differ slightly (Appendix C). Intervals are unadjusted for multiple comparisons. The benchmark texts predate the models, so contamination cannot be ruled out.

Broader Impact Statement

Compaction that deletes a question’s evidence can make supported answers “unsupported”. Without provenance, a downstream consumer may take them for answers that are genuinely unsupported or false, and the sufficiency check does not flag every such case. Recoverable full-state designs should be evaluated before compaction is used in consequential settings. Keeping the full state in turn carries the privacy and retention obligations of whatever it contains. The Evidence Inference articles are clinical-trial reports used only as a benchmark, and compaction and the sufficiency check remain unvalidated for clinical decision support.

Table 3 counts the outcomes by analysis; each prediction, its rule and its estimate are reported in the appendix named in the table. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals, unadjusted for multiple comparisons. The predictions that were not fully met are listed below the table.

Not met.

  • •

  • •

    Follow-up D0: harder LoCoMo options were to bring gpt-6-luna’s empty-memory accuracy to at most 60%; it is 60.2%.

  • •

    τ\tau-bench M2: expected-coverage selection was to lose at most 3 points on the known call by the 90% lower end; ECov −- typed is −-10.6 with lower end −-17.8.

  • •

    τ\tau-bench M3: expected-coverage selection was to close at least 0.70 of the random–oracle gap (G≥0.70G\geq 0.70); it closes G=0.64G=0.64.

  • •

    τ\tau-bench M4: embedding-based expected coverage was to stay within ±3\pm 3 points of the Boolean version; it is −-10.9 [−-18.2, −-4.3] (90%).

  • •
