Appendix B Run details

Texts.

The analyses use, for each MultiRC paragraph, the original text and fifteen compactions (the five sentence policies of Section 2 at three budgets), plus the additional random masks of Appendix C. LLMLingua-2 texts, at 25% and 50%, are read separately (Appendix G).

Coverage and request size.

open-decider’s 75% rows cover 166–171 paragraphs and its other rows, like gpt-6-luna’s, cover 300; open-bosun reads the first 100 paragraphs. The open-weight models are released as decider-2b, bosun-v3.1-1.7b and Lumma-fev-0.6b. The Decisions API accepts at most 200 questions per request, so the 38 read requests above that limit are split into chunks of 125 questions.

Repeat reads.

open-decider reads deterministically up to floating point. Each read is one forward pass in evaluation mode with a softmax over option logits, no sampling and a fixed option order. Each question has its own row, unaffected by the others in the request. Repeated runs of hosted language models can differ (Ouyang et al., 2025; Atıl et al., 2025). For gpt-6-luna, across 100 repeated full-text reads, all 6,603 answers were identical. Its sufficiency checks take few distinct values, which is why ties at the cut are re-read in proportion.

Averages.

Paragraph-macro averages weigh each paragraph equally, with answers averaged within it; bootstrap intervals use 2000 resamples (macro-averaged accuracies and contrasts). The pooled flip-rate risk differences of Section 3 use 1000. The intervals of the sufficiency AUROC against flipped answers and of the re-read gain over a random quarter (MultiRC and FEVER) use 500.

Selection details.

A budget bb keeps max⁡(1,round⁡(b​n))\max(1,\mathrm{round}(bn)) of a paragraph’s nn sentences. The score-based policies keep the highest-scoring sentences, ties going to the earlier sentence. TF-IDF selection fits scikit-learn’s TfidfVectorizer (English stop words, other settings default) on the paragraph’s sentences plus the known question and ranks sentences by cosine similarity to the question.

Refusals.

In the sentence-budget MultiRC reads, 710 of gpt-6-luna’s answers came back as refusals rather than probabilities; they came from 290 requests and were all candidate-answer Booleans. We drop each refused answer from every statistic that needs it. Refusals are rare: under the five sentence policies at 25% and 50%, at most 1.2% of a policy’s known or hidden answers are refused (Table 4a). At token-matched budgets the highest share in the follow-ups is LongLLMLingua’s, 4.8% of hidden answers at 25%; in the granularity test random word deletion draws 6.4% at 25%, so its contrasts rest on the answers it receives. The open-weight readers never refuse.

Counting refusals as wrong changes no contrast’s sign and one detection.

Table 4b recomputes gpt-6-luna’s MultiRC contrasts with each refused answer scored as wrong, with the same paired paragraph bootstrap and seeds. None of the 32 contrasts changes sign. One changes detection: at a token-matched 50% budget, LongLLMLingua falls detectably below random deletion on hidden questions (−-1.4 [−-2.4, −-0.3] points, against −-0.9 [−-1.9, +0.2] with refusals dropped). The largest shift, 2.1 points, is LongLLMLingua’s hidden-question contrast at 25%, where it refuses most.

Typed −- random hidden accuracy at 25% becomes −-1.0 points with one random mask and −-0.4 averaged over masks (refusals dropped: −-0.8 and −-0.2). Known-question accuracy at 25% is 66% after random deletion and 77% after typed selection. The same recomputation for FEVER and Evidence Inference covers 48 contrasts: typed −- random with one mask and averaged over masks, and FEVER’s token-matched contrasts. None changes sign or detection, and the largest shift rounds to 0.03 points.

Evidence details.

ERASER’s evidence sentences were mapped to our segmentation by token overlap (threshold 0.3). At 25% on MultiRC typed selection keeps the full evidence set for 9% (open-decider) and 5% (gpt-6-luna) of hidden questions (paragraph-macro; random 4%). Under random deletion the right-to-wrong rates with evidence intact and broken are 11% and 35% (open-decider) and 5% and 28% (gpt-6-luna).

General instruction-tuned reader.

Reader: plan.

The plan fixed the reader, texts and estimators and two predictions. qwen3.8-flash’s full-text MultiRC accuracy is above the all-“no” rate, with the interval above it (R1), and typed −- random on the known question at 25% is positive on each corpus (R2); hidden contrasts and the overlap split are reported without predictions.

Reader: design.

qwen3.8-flash answers one yes/no question per call, with the paper’s read instructions; the probability of “yes” is taken from the first-token log-probabilities of “yes” and “no” (thinking off) and thresholded at 0.5. It reads the paper’s texts: the full text and typed selection (gpt-6-luna’s selection), question-agnostic selection (MultiRC and FEVER; Evidence Inference has no question-agnostic texts) and random deletion (the paper’s mask) at 25% and 50% of the sentences, and on MultiRC and FEVER the token-matched LLMLingua-2 text at 25%. In all, 337,455 calls; the provider’s content filter refused the answers on 18 MultiRC paragraphs and one FEVER document (0.9–2.8% of MultiRC answers per text), which are dropped as refusals. gpt-6-luna reads the empty text with the paper’s read requests. Estimators are the paper’s.

Reader: results.

Both predictions are met. The full-text accuracy of qwen3.8-flash is 89.2% [88.3, 90.0] on MultiRC (all-“no” 55.6%), 95.1% on FEVER and 91.0% on Evidence Inference. Its contrasts follow those of gpt-6-luna (Table 5): on MultiRC typed selection helps the known question but not hidden questions on average, as overlapping hidden questions gain and disjoint ones lose; on FEVER and Evidence Inference hidden claims gain, and on Evidence Inference disjoint claims gain too. Question-agnostic −- random on hidden questions at 25% is −-0.3 [−-1.4, +0.8] on MultiRC and +2.7 [−-1.1, +6.6] on FEVER. The token-matched LLMLingua-2 text scores 81.3% and 81.3% on hidden questions, against 66.5% and 77.7% for typed selection at 25% of the sentences.

Appendix C Random deletion over several masks

The main text compares each policy with one seeded random mask per paragraph and budget. Here every contrast with random is recomputed against the mean over several seeded masks: 6 per paragraph for gpt-6-luna on MultiRC and FEVER, 11 for open-decider and 4–7 on Evidence Inference, the main mask included. A document’s contrast is the mean over its masks of the paired policy −- random difference, and the bootstrap resamples documents (2000 resamples) and keeps each document’s mask average. Table 6 gives the hidden-question contrasts. On MultiRC the 90% intervals of all 12 hidden-question contrasts with random (the eight of Table 6 and four from open-decider’s re-read) have a largest absolute end of 1.6 points, and typed selection still beats random on the known question (gpt-6-luna +9.7 [+7.2, +11.9] and open-decider +8.6 [+6.0, +11.4] points at 25%). Across single masks, gpt-6-luna’s typed −- random on hidden MultiRC questions at 25% ranges from −-0.8 to +0.3 points, and the main-text mask gives the lowest value. Two cells differ from the one-mask results: the MultiRC disjoint contrast excludes zero in all four reader-budget cells, and the FEVER disjoint contrast at 50% is below random. FEVER agnostic −- random still spans zero at both budgets, and on Evidence Inference H1 remains supported and H2 contradicted. Repeated reads are stable: re-reading the main-text items puts 99.2% of open-decider’s answers on the same side of 0.5, with contrasts on the re-read items within 0.4 points of Table 6, and a repeat of 60 MultiRC paragraphs puts 100.0% of gpt-6-luna’s answers (to one decimal) on the same side.

Appendix D Deleted evidence: the restore experiment and the sufficiency check

Answers flip more often when evidence was deleted.

Of the hidden answers the reader got right on the full text, under typed selection at 25% open-decider flips 14% when their evidence is intact and 36% when it is broken, a difference of +22 [+19, +25] points; for gpt-6-luna the rates are 5% and 29% (+24 [+21, +26]).

gpt-6-luna reads all texts of this experiment. The restore and placebo texts keep the compacted sentences and add the chosen ones, in document order. Each is read with the paragraph’s original question set, split into requests of at most 125 questions as in that read, so only the state differs from the typed-selection 25% read. Recovery rates and accuracies are pooled over candidate answers of broken-evidence hidden questions, not paragraph-macro averages; intervals are paragraph bootstraps (2000 resamples) of the restore −- placebo recovery difference.

Design and results.

On each eligible paragraph let mm be the number of deleted sentences that are evidence for no question and UU the deleted evidence of the broken hidden questions; the dose is d=min⁡(m,|U|)d=\min(m,|U|), and paragraphs with m=0m=0 are skipped (61 of 297). Restore adds dd sentences drawn from UU (seeded per paragraph) and the placebo dd non-evidence sentences, so in 166 paragraphs restore adds only part of the deleted evidence. Restore and placebo reads are interleaved in time. Over 11,296 answers (the 166 answers refused in any of the full, compacted, restore and placebo reads are excluded), accuracy goes from 68% compacted to 78% with restore and 71% with the placebo (full text 89%). Of the 2,795 broken-evidence flips, restore undoes 46% and the placebo 20% (+27 [+23, +32]). On the 801 flips whose question got all its deleted evidence back, the rates are 86% and 21% (+65 [+59, +71]), and on the other 1,994, 31% and 19%. Adding all of the deleted evidence (7.4 sentences on average) against a placebo of as many non-evidence sentences where available (2.6 on average) gives +81 [+78, +84] points over 297 paragraphs.

The sufficiency check.

Every read asks the sufficiency check. We rank the hidden questions by low sufficiency and score the ranking against two outcomes: at least one of the question’s annotated evidence sentences was deleted, and at least one of its candidate answers that was correct on the full text is wrong on the compacted one. These are question-level averages, unlike the paragraph-macro accuracies of the main tables. The re-read simulation gives the lowest-scoring fraction of questions the answers the same reader gave on the full text and compares hidden accuracy with substituting a random share of the same size (paragraph-bootstrap interval on the difference). This equals a real re-read when a second full-text read returns the recorded answer (Appendix B reports repeated reads). Questions tied at the cut are re-read in proportion (the expectation of a random tie-break).

Under typed selection at 25%, the AUROCs against deleted evidence and against flipped answers are 0.81 and 0.69 for open-decider, and 0.83 and 0.71 for gpt-6-luna. The gap between the two AUROCs comes from the reader: many questions whose evidence is broken are still answered correctly. Most of the recovered accuracy comes from re-reading at all: for gpt-6-luna, re-reading the lowest-sufficiency quarter lifts hidden accuracy (candidate-level, averaged over questions) from 67% to 74%, and a random quarter to 73% (open-decider: 62%, 67% and 66%). Choosing by the check thus adds +1.5 [+1.1, +1.8] and +1.7 [+1.2, +2.2] points over a random quarter. The 95% intervals of the AUROCs against flipped answers are [0.67, 0.71] (open-decider) and [0.69, 0.73] (gpt-6-luna). Under typed selection at 25%, 91% (open-decider) and 96% (gpt-6-luna) of hidden questions lost at least one evidence sentence (question-pooled). Re-reading half the questions gains +2.1 and +2.9 points over a random half and lifts that accuracy to 71% and 81% (full text 76% and 89%).

Appendix E FEVER and Evidence Inference: data and the overlap split

FEVER.

At 25% typed selection’s known-claim accuracy is 92% (full text 92%, random 56%). Agnostic −- random on the hidden claims is +2.1 [−-1.7, +5.8] points at 25% and +3.5 [−-0.2, +7.1] at 50%. At 25%, hidden claims judged correctly on the full text flip at 45% when their evidence was broken and 1% when it survived. Unlike on MultiRC, the sufficiency check ranks flipped claims better (AUROC 0.87 [0.85, 0.88]) than deleted evidence (0.77), and re-reading its lowest quarter lifts question-level accuracy from 71% to 86% (random 77%), a gain of +8.9 [+8.3, +9.4] points over a random quarter.

Each read asks, per claim, “given the passage, is this claim supported?” and the sufficiency check. The 200 documents (14.7 sentences and 28.2 claims on average, one sentence per line) are a seeded sample of the ERASER FEVER documents with 8–40 sentences and no empty line that carry at least 3 distinct claims. All but 4 claims have a single label (SUPPORTS or REFUTES) and sentence-level evidence lying entirely in that document (71% of claims are SUPPORTS). A claim’s evidence is the union of its annotated rationale groups. Claims keep the dataset’s file order. Read requests carry at most 100 claims (200 questions, the API limit). For the reported conditions gpt-6-luna answered 400 scoring requests (5,880 sentence Booleans, 0 refused) and 1,809 read requests (50,733 claim answers and 50,733 sufficiency checks, 0 refused), with 20,142,083 input tokens. The data are available under the license terms of the Wikipedia article pages or, where unavailable, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Evidence Inference.

Before any request of this experiment, we specified the corpus, the eligibility and sampling rules, a sample-size rule (the longest prefix of a seeded article order whose expected spend fits a fixed budget), the prompts, policies and budgets, the overlap definition, both hypotheses with their directions, tests and level, the estimand and the bootstrap seed, and which outcomes are exploratory, among them the evidence retention of Table 8.

The data are ERASER’s release (DeYoung et al., 2020) of Evidence Inference (Lehman et al., 2019): full-text clinical-trial articles, one sentence per line, with prompts naming an intervention II, a comparator CC and an outcome OO, a three-way label and annotated evidence sentences. Each prompt becomes the claim “Compared with CC, II produced a statistically significant difference in OO.” The claim is true when the label is a significant increase or decrease and false for no significant difference (55% of the 3,707 claims are true; 112 sentences and 4.7 claims per article on average). The first prompt in file order is known; of the 2,915 hidden claims, 759 overlap the known claim’s evidence and 2,156 do not. Scoring and reading prompts are those of FEVER with the claim text substituted. gpt-6-luna answered 4,752 requests (34,695,247 input tokens, $3.47) with 37,070 read answers, of which 1 was a refusal.

Both hypotheses are one-sided tests at nominal level 0.05 on 2000 article-bootstrap means of the paired typed −- random difference, each decided by the share of means on the wrong side of zero, with 50% as a secondary replication. H1 (overlapping claims, difference >0>0) is supported at both budgets (+21.4 points at 25%, +7.0 at 50%). H2 (disjoint claims, difference ≤0\leq 0) is contradicted at both budgets: disjoint claims gain +9.8 [+7.4, +12.1] points at 25% and +3.9 [+2.0, +5.9] at 50%, and the share of bootstrap means at or below zero is <0.0005<0.0005 at each. Table 8 gives the exploratory unsplit contrast. Hidden accuracy at 25% is 92% (overlapping) and 80% (disjoint) under typed selection, 71% and 70% under random deletion, and 91% and 89% on the full text; the known claim is answered at 91%, 70% and 90%.

Evidence kept (exploratory).

On the overlapping questions typed selection keeps more evidence than random, and they gain, on every corpus. Of the disjoint questions’ evidence (Table 8, last column) it keeps far more than random on Evidence Inference, and they gain; about as much on FEVER, with no detectable gain at 25%; and less on MultiRC, where they lose accuracy. The gain on overlapping questions is also larger on FEVER, so the overlap share is not the only difference behind the main contrast between MultiRC and FEVER. At 25% typed selection keeps, of the overlapping questions’ evidence, 54% and 36% on MultiRC (open-decider, gpt-6-luna), 76% on FEVER and 89% on Evidence Inference, against 25%, 24% and 23% for random; of the disjoint questions’ evidence it keeps the shares in Table 8. Random is the expectation for a uniform subset of the same size on MultiRC and FEVER, and the random policy’s kept set on Evidence Inference. At 50% on Evidence Inference it keeps 94% and 67% (random 50% and 47%).

Appendix F A different known question

Plan.

The plan fixed the choice of the new known question, the policies, readers, budgets and estimators, and four predictions at 25%. Typed beats random deletion on the known question in every corpus–reader cell, with the interval above 0 (K1). On hidden MultiRC questions typed −- random is within ±\pm2 points by the 90% interval, for each reader (K2). Overlapping hidden questions gain more than disjoint ones in every cell, by the estimate (K3). Finally, the line 0.366×0.366\times extra evidence + 0.343+\,0.343 fits the new groups: a line fitted to them has slope above 0, and the fixed line’s mean absolute error is below 4 points (K4).

Design.

In each document the new known question is drawn uniformly, with a seed fixed per document, from the eligible questions other than the first listed one; all other questions, the first one included, are hidden. On FEVER the 4 claims listed with both labels are not eligible, as for hidden claims; the plan does not state this exclusion, and every document has an alternative. This gives 300 MultiRC paragraphs, 200 FEVER documents and 792 Evidence Inference articles. Typed selection is scored again with the new known question and read again at 25% and 50%, with each MultiRC reader scoring for itself. Random deletion keeps the paper’s masks and reads, since its texts do not depend on the known question and each read answers every question; only the overlap labels change. Estimators are the paper’s, with 2000 document resamples. Repeated reads keep 99.2% of open-decider’s and 100.0% of gpt-6-luna’s answers on the same side of 0.5 (Appendix C).

Results.

All four predictions are met (Table 9); the 90% intervals of K2 are [−-1.4, +0.5] (gpt-6-luna) and [−-1.7, +0.4] (open-decider). The line fitted to the new cells has slope 0.416 [0.369, 0.462] and intercept −-1.49. The largest misses are MultiRC overlapping questions with open-decider (predicted +11.4, observed +4.5) and FEVER overlapping claims (predicted +20.1, observed +29.6). On the hidden questions that are hidden under both known questions, typed −- random at 25% is −-0.6 (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna), −-0.6 (MultiRC, open-decider), +15.5 (FEVER) and +12.6 (Evidence Inference) points. At 50%, typed −- random on the known question is +8.7 [+5.8, +11.4] and on hidden questions +0.3 [−-0.9, +1.4] on MultiRC (gpt-6-luna).

Appendix G LLMLingua-2 and other compressors at sentence and token budgets

Setup.

We use microsoft/llmlingua-2-xlm-roberta-large-meetingbank with llmlingua 0.2.2, calling compress_prompt on each document with no question, at rate round⁡(b​n)/n\mathrm{round}(bn)/n for a document of nn sentences, the sentence share of a random bb-budget subset, as a nominal target. Realized token shares are below. The compressed text is read with the same prompts, readers and documents as the sentence policies. LLMLingua-2 −- random contrasts pair it with random deletion averaged over the seeded masks of Appendix C; typed −- LLMLingua-2 contrasts pair it with the main-text typed-selection read. At 25% it keeps 23.5%, 24.7% and 26.1% of the tokens on MultiRC, FEVER and Evidence Inference by its own tokenizer (23.3, 24.6 and 25.8% in o200k tokens), and 27.9%, 25.9% and 26.4% of the characters (random deletion 24.8%, 24.5% and 25.2%). The two are matched in nominal retained share, not in tokens; the follow-up below repeats the comparison at exactly matched token counts. It keeps 20.1%, 20.2% and 20.8% of the words. Word shares count LLMLingua-2’s own word units, and whitespace-separated words for the sentence policies, so comparisons between the two are approximate.

Evidence kept.

At 25% LLMLingua-2 keeps 21.8%, 23.2% and 21.4% of the words of hidden questions’ evidence sentences (MultiRC, FEVER, Evidence Inference), against 23.8%, 23.8% and 24.8% for random deletion and 23.5%, 57.9% and 57.9% for typed selection. For the known question it keeps 21.6%, 23.7% and 20.3%, where typed selection keeps 49.4%, 80.3% and 95.6%. It thus keeps evidence words at roughly the random rate, but spread across most sentences: 92.2%, 96.4% and 93.9% of sentences keep at least one word, with each kept word placed in its sentence. Appendix H separates this spread from the scores.

On the known claim at 25% typed selection beats LLMLingua-2 on FEVER and Evidence Inference (Table 10). On MultiRC the difference is not detected with open-decider (+1.7 [−-1.3, +4.8]), and with gpt-6-luna LLMLingua-2 is better (−-3.0 [−-5.9, −-0.1]). At 25% on the hidden questions LLMLingua-2 answers 80.3% (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna), 81.3% (FEVER) and 69.8% (Evidence Inference).

Follow-up plan.

One plan fixed four follow-ups with their comparisons, decision rules and budgets (A1–D2b). A: typed beats random deletion on the known question in every corpus, reader and budget (A1); on hidden MultiRC questions it is within ±\pm2 points of random by the 90% interval, for each reader and budget (A2a); on hidden FEVER claims it beats random (A2b). B: if LongLLMLingua and MMR beat random on the known question and stay within the margin or below it on hidden questions, the MultiRC hidden result is attributed to conditioning on the known question. C1 and D0–D2b are stated with their results in Appendices J and M. Estimators and bootstrap units are the paper’s: document-macro accuracy, paired contrasts that drop an answer refused in either arm (on LoCoMo a refusal counts as wrong, as in Appendix M), 2000 document resamples (conversations on LoCoMo). Random deletion at token budgets averages three seeded masks per document, computed as in Appendix C. Follow-ups A and B are reported here, C in Appendix J and D in Appendix M.

Token-matched budgets.

A document’s budget is T=round⁡(b​n)T=\mathrm{round}(b\,n) tokens, where nn is the length of its full text under the tiktoken o200k_base encoding and b∈{25,50}%b\in\{25,50\}\%. A sentence policy adds whole sentences in its rank order while the count stays at most TT. It then cuts the first sentence that does not fit to the remaining tokens and stops; the pieces stay in document order. Typed and question-agnostic selection rank by the paper’s scores (on MultiRC, each reader by its own), TF-IDF selection by similarity to the known question, random deletion by a seeded permutation. For LLMLingua-2 and LongLLMLingua, the compression rate (or target length) is bisected to the smallest setting whose output reaches TT tokens, and the output is cut to TT. Every text is within 1 token of its target. LongLLMLingua (Jiang et al., 2024) runs llmlingua 0.2.2 with Llama-2-7B as its scoring model, the sentences as contexts and the known question (or claim) as the query, with document order kept and the library’s settings otherwise. MMR (Carbonell & Goldstein, 1998) ranks sentences greedily by 0.50.5 times the cosine to the query minus 0.50.5 times the largest cosine to a sentence already chosen, with bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings (Xiao et al., 2024). Reads use the paper’s prompts: gpt-6-luna on MultiRC and FEVER and open-decider on MultiRC.

Outcomes A and B.

On the known question typed −- random is +11.4 and +7.0 (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna, 25% and 50%), +7.9 and +6.9 (open-decider) and +35.7 and +20.8 (FEVER), every interval above zero (A1). On hidden FEVER claims it is +17.8 [+15.0, +20.8] and +10.4 [+7.9, +13.0] (A2b). Table 11 gives the accuracies on both question types and Table 12 the contrasts with random deletion on hidden questions. As predicted, typed selection beats random deletion on the known question in every corpus, reader and budget. On hidden questions it is within ±\pm2 points of random on MultiRC (90% interval within that margin in 4 of 4 contrasts; at 25%, [−-1.3, +0.4] with gpt-6-luna and [−-2.0, −-0.3] with open-decider) and above it on FEVER. With open-decider at 25% it is also detectably below random. MMR is within the margin in 4 of 4 contrasts and LongLLMLingua in 1, with the other cells below random. Both beat random deletion on the known question except LongLLMLingua with open-decider at 50% (+1.5 [−-1.0, +4.0]). On FEVER, all query-aware selectors gain on hidden claims, as typed selection does at sentence budgets (Section 3).

Appendix H Word-level compression: the granularity test and the hybrid

LLMLingua-2 differs from random sentence deletion in two ways: it deletes words, so most sentences keep some words, and it chooses them by its scores. This experiment changes one at a time.

The known question.

On the known MultiRC question with gpt-6-luna, typed −- LLMLingua-2 is −-2.3 [−-4.9, +0.6] and −-1.9 [−-3.8, −-0.02] points at matched tokens (25% and 50%), and −-3.0 [−-5.9, −-0.1] and −-2.3 [−-4.3, −-0.2] at the sentence share (Table 10): LLMLingua-2 is ahead in all four comparisons; the two intervals at the sentence share exclude zero, and the one at 50% of the tokens just excludes it (upper end −0.02-0.02 points). With open-decider, typed selection is ahead at 50% (+3.5 [+1.0, +6.0] at matched tokens) and the 25% intervals span zero. On the known FEVER claim typed selection is ahead (+13.0 [+7.5, +18.5]).

Plan.

The plan fixed the policies, contrasts, readers and budgets below and predicted at 25% that contrasts 1 (G1) and 2 (G2) are positive in each cell, with the interval above 0.

Policies.

Every text has the token budget TT of Appendix G, to within 1 token. Four policies fill it:

  • •

    Word scores: the LLMLingua-2 text of Appendix G.

  • •

    Sentence scores: the same model, with no question. A word’s score is its keep probability in compress_prompt (the “preserve” probability averaged over its tokens), and a sentence’s score is the mean over its words. Sentences are added in descending score, ties in document order, as for the sentence policies of Appendix G.

  • •

    Random words: whitespace-separated words are added in a seeded random order until the budget is reached, then kept in document order. Each document has three masks.

  • •

    Random sentences: the random deletion of Appendix G, with its three masks.

The four contrasts are (1) word scores −- sentence scores, (2) random words −- random sentences, (3) sentence scores −- random sentences and (4) word scores −- random words. Contrasts 1 and 2 change only the unit of deletion, contrasts 3 and 4 only whether the scores choose. Readers, prompts and estimators are those of Appendix G: paired, document-macro accuracy on hidden questions, with 2000 document resamples. A random policy’s value for a document is the mean over its three masks.

Results.

Prediction 1 is met in all three cells: at 25%, word scores −- sentence scores is +4.6 points (MultiRC, open-decider), +11.7 (MultiRC, gpt-6-luna) and +19.1 (FEVER; Table 13). Prediction 2 is met with gpt-6-luna, with random words −- random sentences at +1.2 points on MultiRC and +6.3 on FEVER, but not with open-decider (+0.4 [−-0.4, +1.3]). Applied to whole sentences, the scores are not detectably better than random sentences in five of the six cells; the exception is open-decider at 25% (+1.3 [+0.2, +2.3]). Applied to words, they beat random words in every cell. The LLMLingua-2 advantage thus comes mainly from its scores choosing words. Keeping words spread over nearly every sentence without the scores adds less (contrast 2 against contrast 4), and with open-decider no gain is detected.

What the texts keep.

At 25%, the two word policies leave at least one word in 92.9% and 94.5% of MultiRC sentences (FEVER: 95.2% and 98.3%). The two sentence policies keep 32.6% and 29.3% of sentences (FEVER: 29.6% and 29.5%). The four keep similar shares of the words of hidden questions’ evidence sentences on MultiRC (word scores 26.3%, sentence scores 28.4%, random words 25.0%, random sentences 26.1%). On FEVER sentence scores keep the most (35.7%, against 26.4%, 25.2% and 25.7%) and are still less accurate than both word policies on hidden claims (63.1%, against 82.2% for word scores and 67.5% for random words). Word scores and random words keep about the same share of evidence words, so what the scores add is the choice of which words to keep.

The hybrid compactor.

The plan, written before any request of this experiment, asked whether a compaction that keeps the known question’s evidence as whole sentences and a few scored words of every other sentence beats typed selection on hidden questions while staying ahead of LLMLingua-2 on the known one. At the token budget TT of the follow-ups (Appendix G), the hybrid first adds whole sentences in typed-selection order (each reader’s own typed scores) while they stay within a​TaT, with a=0.5a=0.5 (primary) or 0.250.25 (secondary); it then fills the remaining budget with the other sentences’ words in order of LLMLingua-2 keep probability (the scores of the granularity test, no question), keeping all pieces in document order. Typed selection, LLMLingua-2, random sentences and random words (three masks each) are re-read in the same run, so no contrast mixes runs. Estimators are the follow-ups’. Table 14 gives the 25% accuracies and evidence kept. The plan predicted, in each of the three cells, that the hybrid beats typed selection on hidden questions (H1), beats LLMLingua-2 on the known question (H2) and is at most 2 points below LLMLingua-2 on hidden questions by the 90% lower end (H3). Hybrid −- typed, hidden, is +8.3 [+7.0, +9.5] (MultiRC, luna), +4.6 [+3.5, +5.8] (dec) and +5.7 [+3.6, +7.8] (FEVER): H1 is met in all three. Hybrid −- LLMLingua-2, known, is +1.3 [−-1.0, +3.4], +0.7 [−-1.8, +3.5] and +9.5 [+3.0, +15.5]: H2 is not met, not met and met. Hybrid −- LLMLingua-2, hidden, is −-4.2 [−-5.1, −-3.3], −-2.4 [−-3.2, −-1.5] and +2.6 [+0.7, +4.5] (90% intervals): H3 is not met, not met and met. The quarter-budget hybrid was planned without a prediction.

Appendix I Content-word evidence retention (exploratory)

This analysis was not planned in advance and uses only the texts and reads of the hybrid experiment (Appendix H); it sends no new request. A word is a content word if, lower-cased and stripped of surrounding punctuation, it contains a letter or digit and is not in scikit-learn’s English stop list. For each hidden question and compacted text we measure four shares. All words and content are the shares of its annotated evidence’s words and content words kept. Breadth is the share of its evidence sentences with at least one content word kept, and, on MultiRC, answer is the share of each candidate answer’s content words that occur in the kept text. The unit is one candidate answer (MultiRC) or claim (FEVER) in one compacted text, scored right or wrong, with refusals dropped and weights that make every document and policy count once. A linear probability model with document fixed effects and policy indicators pools the six policies of a cell; a feature enters as indicators of gold label by feature bin (0 and 1 are their own bins, interior values are cut at their pooled deciles) or, in the linear form, as one slope per gold label. The policy gap left after conditioning is the difference of policy coefficients, with 2000 document-bootstrap resamples.

The FEVER evidence-support check of Section 4 uses the binary reads. A claim’s target is “supported” if it is true and its evidence is fully kept (all evidence sentences for sentence policies, all evidence content words for word policies), “not supported” if its evidence is entirely deleted, and undefined otherwise; accuracy weights the two targets equally. Unlike the three-way target of Appendix J, it leaves a false claim with fully kept evidence undefined, so the FEVER typed −- random contrast covers fewer claims (3,685 against 4,528). The label split of Section 4 covers 3,850 true and 1,582 false hidden claims; the bin with at most a fifth of the evidence content words kept holds 458 true claims after LLMLingua-2 and 2,575 after random sentence deletion; the target is defined for 45 of the 5,432 hidden claims answered under LLMLingua-2 (one claim refused there is dropped), for 3,685 claims in the typed −- random contrast and for 1,140 in the hybrid −- typed contrast. The relaxed variant counts evidence as kept above 80% and as deleted below 20% of its content words; under it LLMLingua-2 −- random sentence deletion is −-19.8 [−-29.7, −-12.0] points on the 675 claims where both texts define it.

Table 15 gives the gaps at 25%. Content-word retention lowers every gap and leaves no detected LLMLingua-2 −- random-sentence gap on FEVER. Breadth alone over-corrects: conditioning on it turns several gaps negative, because random word deletion also keeps some word of most evidence sentences yet scores lower. On FEVER the all-word measure, binned, also absorbs most of the LLMLingua-2 gap, because the relation between FEVER accuracy and retention is strongly non-linear; in the linear form content-word retention leaves +14.9 points there, so on FEVER the two measures are not separated.

Appendix J The three-way read and the support target

This prespecified follow-up (C1) re-reads the hidden claims with three answers. C1 predicted that typed selection beats random deletion in label recovery (labels weighted equally) on both corpora at 25%; it does, by +25.2 [+19.9, +30.8] on FEVER and +23.1 [+20.2, +25.9] on Evidence Inference. The texts are those of the paper’s reads (full, typed selection and random deletion at 25% and 50%, the paper’s mask). One request per text asks, for each claim, a Choice among “supported”, “refuted” and “not enough info” (“the passage does not contain enough information to decide the claim”), with no other question. Gold labels: FEVER SUPPORTS and Evidence Inference significant differences are “supported”, the rest “refuted”. Label recovery scores against the document’s label (“not enough info” counts wrong). The support target of a claim in a text is the document’s label if all of the claim’s annotated evidence is kept, “not enough info” if none is, and undefined if part of it is kept (732 of the hidden FEVER claims after typed selection at 25%, 510 on Evidence Inference). Table 16 gives each text’s label-recovery levels over all claims its read answered.

Typed selection and random deletion are compared on a common set (Table 16): for each corpus and budget, the hidden claims that both reads answered and, for the support target, that have a target in both texts. On that set, let at,ℓ,da_{t,\ell,d} be text tt’s accuracy on the claims of document dd whose target in tt is ℓ\ell, and a¯t,ℓ\bar{a}_{t,\ell} its mean over the documents that have such a claim. Text tt scores St=|L|−1​∑ℓ∈La¯t,ℓS_{t}=|L|^{-1}\sum_{\ell\in L}\bar{a}_{t,\ell}, with LL the two labels for recovery and the three for support, and the contrast is Styped−SrandomS_{\text{typed}}-S_{\text{random}} with a 2000-resample document bootstrap. The table’s two levels thus subtract to the contrast up to rounding. A claim’s support target can differ between the two texts, so the support contrast compares the reader on the claim mix each text leaves. Typed selection recovers the label more often than random deletion at both budgets on both corpora, as predicted at 25%; the support target had no prediction (Table 16). Comparing the two texts only within documents where both have a claim with a given target (exploratory) gives −-1.6 [−-4.5, +1.6] and −-0.3 [−-3.1, +2.7] at 25% (FEVER, Evidence Inference): on Evidence Inference at 25%, the small support gain depends on this choice. At 50% on Evidence Inference, the support contrast exceeds the label contrast.

Appendix K The prespecified KEEP–DROP contrast

Before any request of this experiment, we specified the corpora, the two arms, the reader and prompt, the size-based exclusion, the estimand, the bootstrap seeds, both predictions with their test and level, and which outcomes are descriptive. Only item construction and token counting, which use sentence sets alone, came first.

Design.

The sample is every document already read under typed selection at 25%: 200 FEVER documents and 792 Evidence Inference articles. Let KK be typed selection’s kept set, k=|K|k=|K|, and EE the union of a hidden claim’s annotated rationale groups. KEEP is KK with E∖KE\setminus K added and as many sentences of K∖EK\setminus E removed, lowest typed-selection score first; DROP is KK with K∩EK\cap E removed and as many sentences drawn uniformly (seeded per claim) from outside K∪EK\cup E added. Both have kk sentences in document order; KEEP holds all of EE and DROP none of it, and when KK already holds all of EE (or none), KEEP (or DROP) is KK itself. Sentences swapped in or out may be evidence for other claims, so the two arms can differ in more than the claim’s evidence. Averaged over the analyzed hidden claims (a claim mean, unlike the retention shares of Table 8), KK already holds 49% of a hidden claim’s evidence on FEVER and 57% on Evidence Inference. gpt-6-luna answers one claim per request with the claim and sufficiency checks of the main reads, worded as before; a claim counts as correct when its probability is on the side of its gold label. All 16,102 requests were sent as one shuffled list, so arms and corpora are interleaved in time (15,135,563 input tokens, $1.51).

Exclusions.

Hidden claims are those with a single gold label (Appendix E): the 4 FEVER claims that the source lists for the same document as both SUPPORTS and REFUTES are not among them. This exclusion is not in the plan and changes no decision. Thus 16,094 of the 16,102 requests enter the analysis. A claim with |E|>k|E|>k has no KEEP with the same number of sentences. This leaves 5,132 of the 5,433 FEVER hidden claims and all 2,915 on Evidence Inference. Every eligible pair was answered, and none was refused; Table 17 gives the analyzed pairs (nn).

Tests.

The estimand is the mean over documents of each document’s mean correct(KEEP) −- correct(DROP), with 2000 document-bootstrap resamples. The plan makes two predictions per corpus, KEEP −- DROP >0>0 on all hidden claims and on the disjoint ones, each tested one-sided at nominal level 0.05 by the share of bootstrap means at or below zero; the overlapping claims are a secondary test. Both predictions are supported on both corpora (KD1 and KD2 on FEVER, KD3 and KD4 on Evidence Inference) (Table 17).

Appendix L Token counts and input-token cost

Tokens kept at sentence and turn budgets.

Under the o200k_base encoding, each policy keeps within 5 points of the budget’s share of the tokens, except TF-IDF selection on Evidence Inference (30.4% at 25%, 59.0% at 50%) and question-agnostic selection on LoCoMo (32.3% and 60.6%); typed selection keeps 28.9% and 53.5% on Evidence Inference. KEEP texts are longer than DROP texts: 117 against 106 tokens on FEVER (+10.8 [+8.3, +13.1]), 1,328 against 1,294 on Evidence Inference (+33.2 [+27.3, +39.4]) and 6,252 against 6,225 on LoCoMo (+26.6 [+18.7, +34.2]; document or conversation bootstrap).

Input-token cost.

Table 18 counts gpt-6-luna input tokens per document. Scoring and the batched reads, which ask all of a document’s questions in one request, are measured. Per-question costs are modeled for one-question requests by a token model fitted to each corpus’s recorded requests (on MultiRC, scoring and batched reads of about 60 questions each only, so its one-question costs are an extrapolation; mean absolute error 2.2% on FEVER, 8.2% on Evidence Inference and 1.6% on LoCoMo). With batched reads, scoring plus the 25% read costs 1.15, 1.23, 3.94 and 2.53 times the full read (MultiRC, FEVER, Evidence Inference, LoCoMo). With one request per later question, compacting once costs 1.05, 0.62, 1.55 and 0.33 times always reading the full text at each corpus’s mean number of later questions k¯\bar{k}. Adding the sufficiency check and a full re-read for a quarter of the questions raises this to 1.42, 1.12, 1.83 and 0.59 with the check in the read request.

Appendix M The LoCoMo agent-memory test

KEEP beats DROP.

At the last checkpoint, gpt-6-luna answers a hidden question more accurately from the typed 25% memory with its evidence (KEEP) than from one with the same number of turns without it (DROP). KEEP −- DROP is +13.3 points, positive in all 10 conversations, on all questions and on the 1,408 evidence-disjoint ones, so H2a and H2b are supported. Read by qwen3.8-flash, the same texts also meet H2’s decision rule (+10.7 [+8.3, +13.3] on all questions). The four options include no “not supported” answer, so missing evidence cannot make the reader right by default.

Typed versus random deletion is unresolved at 25%.

With empty memory at 81.4%, absolute differences are small. H1, typed −- random hidden accuracy at 25%, is unresolved for both readers, and so is the typed −- random difference in evidence kept. H3, which asks the first to follow the second, therefore cannot be assessed. H4 is supported: low sufficiency ranks hidden questions with dropped evidence first (AUROC 0.81 [0.79, 0.84]). Question-agnostic selection keeps more of hidden questions’ evidence turns than typed selection (48.6% against 27.2% at 25%), but also longer turns (Appendix L). With harder answer options, in a prespecified follow-up, KEEP still beats DROP and typed versus random stays unresolved (Table 20).

Plan, data and cost.

Before any request of this experiment, we specified the data, checkpoints, known-question rule, policies, read format, readers, the four hypotheses with their tests, the bootstrap seed and the outcomes reported without a decision rule. Only item construction and token estimation (no model answer) came first. The data are locomo10.json from the authors’ repository (Maharana et al., 2024) at commit 3eb6f2c, released under CC BY-NC 4.0; our use is non-commercial research, and we use the released photo captions as text. gpt-6-luna cost $5.08 (50,816,715 input tokens) and qwen3.8-flash $12.10 (80,631,483 prompt tokens).

Design.

Eligible questions are LoCoMo’s categories 1–4 (multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, single-hop) with a gold answer and at least one valid evidence turn, 1,536 in all; adversarial questions have no gold answer. Memory is rendered as session blocks, each headed by its session’s date, then one line per kept turn with its speaker and any photo caption. Headers do not count against the budget, since temporal answers are relative to session dates. With SS sessions, checkpoint kk closes session ⌈k​S/4⌉\lceil kS/4\rceil. The known question at kk is, among unused eligible questions whose last evidence turn lies in segment kk, the one with the smallest CRC32 checksum of a fixed key. At checkpoint kk with NkN_{k} turns seen, a policy keeps round⁡(b​Nk)\mathrm{round}(bN_{k}) of the previous memory plus the new turns, and a dropped turn never returns. Typed and agnostic use gpt-6-luna scores with the known- and agnostic-policy wording of the earlier corpora, “sentence” replaced by “turn”; TF-IDF, random and lead are as before, recency keeps the latest turns. Hidden questions at kk are every eligible question whose evidence lies before checkpoint kk, except the conversation’s four known questions: 351, 671, 1,061 and 1,496 at k=1,…,4k=1,\dots,4. The three distractors of a question are answers to other questions of the same conversation, same category first, with near-duplicates excluded and the option order fixed by a hash. gpt-6-luna reads up to 100 questions per request, each with the Choice and the sufficiency check (“does the conversation memory contain the information needed to answer this question?”). qwen3.8-flash answers one question per call from first-token log-probabilities over the option letters (thinking off), at the last checkpoint, for typed, TF-IDF, random and recency at 25%, full and empty memory, on gpt-6-luna’s selections. A refusal counts as wrong; dropping instead every question refused under either memory condition of a contrast changes no planned decision.

Tests.

Every estimate is the mean over conversations of the per-conversation mean paired difference, with 2000 conversation-bootstrap resamples. H1 (two-sided) is positive or negative if the 95% interval excludes zero and unresolved otherwise; H2a and H2b (one-sided, nominal level 0.05) are supported if the 5th percentile is above zero. KEEP is the typed 25% memory at the last checkpoint with the question’s missing evidence added and as many non-evidence turns removed, lowest typed score first. DROP removes its kept evidence and adds as many turns drawn at random from outside the memory and the evidence. Each of the 2,992 KEEP and DROP reads asks one question, in one shuffled list. H3 is consistent or inconsistent only if H1 and the typed −- random retention difference are both resolved. H4 is supported if the 2.5th percentile of a conversation bootstrap of the pooled AUROC exceeds 0.5. With ten clusters the percentile bootstrap may under-cover. Pooled over questions, KEEP scores 97.7% and DROP 85.1%.

Test results.

H1, typed −- random at 25%, is −-0.4 [−-2.1, +1.0] with gpt-6-luna and +0.6 [−-1.8, +2.8] with qwen3.8-flash, both unresolved. KEEP −- DROP is +13.3 [+10.9, +16.4] on all hidden questions (H2a, supported) and +13.3 [+10.7, +16.8] on evidence-disjoint ones (H2b, supported). The conversation-macro typed −- random difference in evidence kept is +2.1 [−-2.5, +6.5], so H3 is not assessable. The sufficiency AUROC against dropped evidence is 0.81 [0.79, 0.84] (H4, supported).

Second reader.

In the plan qwen3.8-flash reads six memory conditions to replicate H1; its KEEP–DROP reads are an exploratory extension under H2’s decision rule. qwen3.8-flash read the same 1,496 KEEP and DROP pairs, one question per call, with no refusals. KEEP −- DROP is +10.7 [+8.3, +13.3] points on all questions (90.8% vs. 80.5%; 5th percentile +8.6), +10.6 [+8.0, +13.3] on the 1,408 disjoint ones (5th percentile +8.5) and +9.1 [+4.1, +15.2] on the 88 overlapping ones, positive in 10, 10 and 6 of ten conversations. Both 5th percentiles are above zero, so the H2a and H2b rules are also met on this reader. The accuracies in parentheses are question-pooled and the contrasts conversation-macro, so they need not subtract exactly.

Empty memory already answers most questions.

The two readers answer 81.4% and 85.1% of hidden questions from empty memory (full memory 96.8% and 96.6%). The distractors are answers to other questions of the same conversation, and they can often be ruled out; the prespecified follow-up with harder options (below) lowers this floor.

Harder options (follow-up D).

With harder options, empty memory drops to 60.2% (gpt-6-luna) and 71.5% (qwen3.8-flash; Table 20). Only the three wrong options of each question change; questions, memories and KEEP/DROP texts are those of Section 5. For temporal questions and questions asking how many, how long or when, the wrong options are the gold answer with its date shifted by one to four weeks (same month first) or its number shifted (21.1% of wrong options). Otherwise they are answers to questions of the same form (same head noun or opening words), ranked by TF-IDF similarity of the questions. They come from other conversations if they name no speaker (59.5%), or from the same conversation if their question is not a near duplicate (17.0%). Yes/no answers keep the original options (2.3%). The plan set a target of at most 60% question-pooled empty-memory accuracy for gpt-6-luna. The construction reaches a question-pooled 60.2% (original options 82.2%), missing the target by 0.2 points. Table 20 gives, per memory and reader, the refusal rate, the accuracy over all questions (refusals wrong) and the accuracy over answered questions. Full-memory accuracy falls to 90.9% (original options: 96.8%), since a shifted date can be hard to rule out even with the whole conversation. The plan applies the rules of H1 (D1) and H2a and H2b (D2a, D2b). Typed −- random at 25% is +1.3 [−-1.7, +4.3] (gpt-6-luna) and +0.2 [−-2.9, +3.2] (qwen3.8-flash), unresolved. KEEP −- DROP is +18.5 [+15.6, +21.3] and +14.7 [+10.7, +18.8], and on evidence-disjoint questions +18.7 [+15.8, +21.5] and +15.1, supported for both readers. Dropping refused answers (exploratory) leaves every decision unchanged.

Appendix N The τ\tau-bench test

Selectors and results.

The sample has 390 states from 81 tasks with 837 hidden questions, excluding the trajectories of a pilot. Budgets keep 25% of the tokens, and intervals bootstrap tasks. Besides the selectors above, an oracle keeps the units most hidden questions need. Two selectors anticipate later calls. Anticipatory selection keeps units needed by any of ten likely later questions that qwen3.8-flash writes from the state, and expected-coverage selection (ECov) weighs those questions against the known one (below). Of 13 prespecified predictions, 8 are met (Table 3).

Typed selection beats random deletion on hidden questions.

Typed −- random is +22.3 [+15.1, +28.9] points with gpt-6-luna and +21.7 [+15.7, +27.6] with qwen3.8-flash (Table 21), unlike on MultiRC. Typed selection also keeps the hidden question’s identifier more often (66.4% against 42.4%), and hidden questions whose identifier survives score 85.9%, against 18.9% when it is lost. This association is consistent with the relation between gain and evidence kept of Section 3. LLMLingua-2 keeps the identifier for 52.3% and shows no detected gain (+4.0 [−-1.1, +9.3]). Recency, which keeps the newest units, gains +9.1 points on hidden questions but scores only 28.9% on the known one, because the identifiers sit in earlier units.

Anticipating later calls costs the known question.

ECov −- typed is +12.8 [+5.2, +20.8] on hidden questions but −-10.6 (90% interval [−-17.8, −-2.9]) on the known one; anticipatory selection gives +8.7 and −-12.0. No selector we tested beats typed selection on both. Fetching dropped units on demand also stays well below the full state at about the same passage tokens (recoverable arm below).

Sample and questions.

The trajectories are the successful (reward 1) retail trajectories of the two agents whose histories τ\tau-bench releases (MIT license); airline trajectories (41 states) are descriptive only: gpt-6-luna scores 76.7% (full), 66.8% (typed), 60.0% (random) and 27.2% (empty) on its hidden questions. The plan, with its predictions, was written before any request. The 40 pilot trajectories were inspected to choose the newest-first tie-break of anticipatory selection and are excluded. The checkpoint is the middle tool output. Questions whose gold identifier is ambiguous, not identifier-like or a bare list entry are dropped, and in quoted text every substring with the gold’s character pattern is masked. In six retail hidden questions a later user turn gives the identifier without its leading “#”, which this mask misses; dropping them moves typed −- random and LLMLingua-2 −- random by at most 0.2 points. A known question exists when the next call’s identifier argument occurs in the state with at least one same-shaped distractor (407 known questions, one per identifier argument of the next call). A refusal counts as wrong; the full-state refusal rate is 1.9% (95% upper limit 2.9%), so the prespecified validity check passes. Other arms refuse more often (retail, gpt-6-luna): random 16.0%, LLMLingua-2 16.2%, typed 10.9%, anticipatory 6.4%, ECov 6.9% and empty 66.7%. On answered questions only, typed −- random is +23.0 [+17.4, +27.8], LLMLingua-2 −- random +4.0 [−-1.2, +8.9], ECov −- typed +5.8 [−-1.4, +13.6], anticipatory −- typed +2.9 [−-1.5, +8.0] and recency −- random +4.4 [−-1.8, +11.2] points on hidden questions.

Selectors.

Budgets are T=round(0.25×T=\mathrm{round}(0.25\times the state’s o200k tokens)), filled unit by unit in rank order. Typed selection ranks units by gpt-6-luna’s probability that the unit is needed for the known question; typed, newest-first breaks its ties toward newer units. ECov adds units greedily by their gain in F⁡(S)=∑qwq​[1−∏u∈S(1−p⁡(u,q))]F(S)=\sum_{q}w_{q}\,[1-\prod_{u\in S}(1-p(u,q))], with weight 0.5 on the known question (pp = the typed probability) and 0.05 on each of the ten generated questions (pp from a gpt-6-luna Boolean per unit and question). ECov-embed replaces the latter by a logistic function of the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine between unit and question. Hybrid keeps typed whole units up to half the budget and fills the rest with LLMLingua-2 words. Gist writes every unit as a numbered line holding its top LLMLingua-2 words within 60% of the budget, then restores typed whole units. Table 21 gives these arms; their predictions are under Prespecified predictions below. Under recency the newest unit takes a median 8.5% of the budget, and the rest of its budget goes to the next-newest units.

Prespecified predictions.

Hidden questions unless stated (M1–M4 on the ECov subsample): ECov −- typed is +12.8 [+5.2, +20.8] (M1, at least +5+5 with the interval above 0: met); on the known question it is −-10.6 [−-17.8, −-2.9] (90%; M2, lower end above −3-3: not met); ECov closes G=0.64G=0.64 of the random–oracle gap (M3, G≥0.70G\geq 0.70: not met); ECov-embed −- ECov is −-10.9 [−-18.2, −-4.3] (90%; M4, within ±3\pm 3: not met); ECov −- gist is +26.3 [+16.4, +36.0] (M5, above 0: met); the recoverable gist arm is below (M6, at least 95% of full-state accuracy at no more than 60% of its tokens: not met). Typed −- random is +22.3 [+15.1, +28.9] (T1: met), recency −- random +9.1 [+3.4, +15.4] (T2: met) and anticipatory −- random +31.0 [+24.7, +36.6] (T3: met). Questions whose identifier is kept score +67.0 points above those whose identifier is lost (T4, at least 40: met). LLMLingua-2 keeps fewer identifiers than typed selection (52.3% against 66.4%) and LLMLingua-2 −- typed is −-18.2 points (T6: met). Hybrid −- typed is −-10.4 [−-15.0, −-5.6] (90%; T7, lower end above −2-2: not met). With qwen3.8-flash typed −- random has the same sign as with gpt-6-luna (T9: met).

Recoverable arm.

Dropped units leave either a stub naming the run of dropped units and their roles, or the gist line above, so each unit keeps its position. A hidden question whose sufficiency is below a threshold θ\theta is re-read alone with dropped units added in order of TF-IDF match between the question and what remains visible of them, up to a quarter of the full state’s tokens. With gists at θ=0.5\theta=0.5 it reaches 69.1% against 88.8% for the full state, at 102.0% of the full state’s passage tokens (o200k, without the question and option text) per question (Table 22). Low sufficiency ranks questions whose identifier was dropped first (AUROC 0.73 with stubs, 0.72 with gists), so the main failure is choosing the units to fetch. The first pass reads all questions of a state plus the sufficiency check (Section 3) for each hidden question; it scores 64.0% on hidden questions with stubs and 51.3% with gists. Tokens per question count the first read divided by the state’s hidden questions, plus the re-read. Table 22 gives question-mean accuracy; the full state scores 88.8% on the same questions.

Appendix O Abstractive summaries

Design.

Paragraphs, known questions, reader (gpt-6-luna) and the 25% token budget TT are those of the hybrid test (Appendix H), and random sentence deletion, typed selection and LLMLingua-2 are that test’s reads. Each summarizer writes two summaries per paragraph. The generic prompt asks for a summary “for a reader who will later be asked questions about it that are not known yet”; the focused prompt asks for one “so that the summary answers the question”, followed by the known question. qwen3.8-flash (temperature 0) is asked for at most 0.75​T0.75T words; gpt-6.1-sol (temperature 1, reasoning effort low) is asked for about T/1.25T/1.25 words, close to that length. A summary longer than TT tokens is cut to its first TT tokens. The provider’s input filter rejected qwen3.8-flash requests for 3 paragraphs (focused) and 4 (generic); these drop out of that arm’s contrasts. Estimators are the follow-ups’ (Appendix G).

Plan and results.

A plan written before any request fixed the prompts, the contrasts of Table 23 and two predictions for qwen3.8-flash: the generic summary beats random sentence deletion on hidden questions (S1), and the focused summary beats it on the known question (S2). A second plan, written after that run and before any gpt-6.1-sol summary, added gpt-6.1-sol with S1 and S2, the prediction that its generic summary stays below LLMLingua-2 on hidden questions (S3), and the prediction that both its summaries use a larger share of TT than qwen3.8-flash’s (S4). All six are met (Table 23). On hidden questions gpt-6.1-sol −- qwen3.8-flash is +3.3 [+2.3, +4.3] points for the generic summaries and +3.9 [+3.0, +4.9] for the focused ones; since gpt-6.1-sol also fills more of the budget, the writer and the length are not separated. Of its generic summaries, 74.3% were cut at TT tokens.
